name: Tataltepec Chatino
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Sullivant, John Ryan. 2015. The Phonology and Inflectional Morphology of Cháʔknyá, Tataltepec de Valdés Chatino, a Zapotecan Language. PhD dissertation, University of Texas at Austin (hdl 2152/31493; UT repository via the Internet Archive capture 2022-01-24).
catalog_locator: Ch. 2 sec. 2.2 'Stress', p. 54; sec. 2.2.1 'Phonological consequences of stress', p. 55 and fn. 1; Ch. 3 intro, p. 68; sec. on /β̞/, p. 126; Ch. 4 intro, p. 150.
catalog_quote: All syllables in Tataltepec Chatino are either stressed (σS) or unstressed (σW). Stressed syllables are always stem-final syllables (that is, word-final unless the stem is followed by one or more enclitics), and stem-final syllables are always stressed. ... Tataltepec Chatino and the other languages of Core Chatino (Zenzontepec Chatino and all extant topolects of Eastern Chatino) all share this stem-final stress where disyllabic stems ω are realized as σW σS. Beyond phonetic affects of stress (including greater durations and intensities of σS), there are phonological consequences of stress. Only σS can be long or linked to the [+ nasal] feature, while σW can only be oral and short. ... Each stem is associated with one lexical tone class (which contains a sequence of zero to two tones) and contains one stressed syllable. Person clitics can have their own tone class, but form a phonological constituent with their host in that they do not receive sentence-level stress. Stressed syllables are the stem-final syllables where the number of phonemic contrasts is greatest. By contrast, unstressed syllables are the penultimate and antepenultimate (or earlier) syllables where the range of possible phonemic contrasts is reduced.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is fixed on the final syllable of the stem, which is the final syllable of the word unless enclitics (e.g. person clitics) follow; enclitics are unstressed and outside the stress domain. Each stem has exactly one stressed syllable; penultimate and earlier syllables are unstressed and show reduced contrasts (no length, no nasality, few mid vowels). Spanish loans are restressed on the final syllable regardless of source stress. The language is also tonal (lexical tone sequences linked right-to-left from the stressed final mora).
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; each stem 'contains one stressed syllable'. In verb compounds the first stem loses its stress (its long vowel shortens), so only the final syllable of the compound is stressed.
new_statements.exceptions: Enclitics (person clitics) do not take stress, so stress is stem-final rather than strictly word-final in cliticized forms; compound verbs have a single stress on the last stem; loans receive final stress. Footnote: non-Core Chatino Zapotecan languages (Soltec, Teojomulco Chatino) had the opposite stem-initial pattern.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the stem/phonological word (ω): stress is stem-final = word-final absent enclitics; clitics form a phonological constituent with the host but are unstressed. Statement is phonological (distributional evidence from length/nasality licensing and compounding) with mention of phonetic correlates (duration, intensity); tone is independent and lexical.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes exactly Tataltepec de Valdés Chatino (Cháʔknyá), glottocode tata1258 / ISO cta; Sullivant notes no prominent internal dialect variation. The same stem-final stress is stated to hold for all Core Chatino (Zenzontepec zenz1235 and Eastern Chatino topolects).

tone_statements.quote: Proto-Chatino (based on Campbell & Woodbury 2010) contrasted *H vs. *L vs. Ø. Most words were bimoraic, and tones linked to morae one-to-one from the end of the word. *H was culminative (max. one H per word). [...] While the modern varieties maintain privativity (Ø) and H culminativity, their tone systems have diverged significantly in terms of inventory, distribution, and processes, as shown in Table 2 (H̋ = extra-high). [Table 2, column Tataltepec:] Inventory of tonal contrasts on the mora | H, L, Ø, H̋, H͡L | # of tonal melodies on the word | 8 | Floating tones | H̋ | Tones that spread | H, L

sources.note: Section 2.2 'Stress' (p.54): stressed syllables are always stem-final syllables (word-final unless followed by enclitics) and stem-final syllables are always stressed; disyllabic stems are sigmaW sigmaS; only stressed syllables host length and nasality contrasts; loans get final stress regardless of Spanish source stress (p.~126); person enclitics form a constituent with the host and do not receive sentence-level stress (p.68). Language is also tonal (Ch.5, eight tone sequences per stem).

sources.note: Gives Tataltepec's synchronic tone system in comparative tables: tonal contrasts on the mora H, L, Ø (toneless), extra-high H̋ and contour H͡L; 8 tonal melodies on the word; a floating extra-high tone; H and L spread; privative (Ø) system with culminative H inherited from Proto-Chatino *H/*L/Ø linked to morae; cognate sets with Tataltepec tone transcriptions and discussion of tone perturbation by the potential-mood H prefix.
